observations.value: linear lucencies in soft tissues of neck and chest wall, especially visible in Figure 1b (lateral view) as black streaks anterior to trachea and along sternum
radiolucent stripe outlining mediastinal structures; in Figure 1b, air is seen anterior to trachea and extending to xiphoid region (white arrow), with sharp delineation at xiphoid attachment
free air under diaphragm, visible in Figure 1a as radiolucency beneath right hemidiaphragm (black arrows)
no obvious discontinuity or sharp angulation of tracheal lumen in either image; trachea appears patent though obscured by overlying structures and air
not clearly present; lung markings extend to periphery bilaterally in Figure 1a; no visible pleural line or apical lucency
no meniscus sign or homogeneous opacity in costophrenic angles; diaphragmatic contours are sharp
mediastinal width appears normal; no significant deviation or enlargement
no double contour of cardiac silhouette or lucent halo around heart
patchy opacities in both lungs, but not clearly confluent or typical for contusion; could represent atelectasis or aspiration

hypotheses.name: Blunt tracheal rupture with air dissection into mediastinum, peritoneum, and subcutaneous tissues
hypotheses.basis: Classic triad of subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum (especially anterior, demarcated by xiphoid), and pneumoperitoneum is highly suggestive of tracheal or bronchial rupture allowing air to track down retroperitoneal planes; absence of pneumothorax supports intrathoracic rupture without pleural breach

hypotheses.name: Esophageal perforation
hypotheses.basis: Can also cause pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema, and pneumoperitoneum; however, typically associated with mediastinal fluid/pleural effusion and may show pleural air; not strongly supported here due to lack of pleural fluid or classic ‘left-sided’ pneumomediastinum
